paragraphs: Class-incremental learning trains a classifier as examples from new classes arrive over time. Updating the model can erase knowledge of earlier classes, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Keeping old examples available for retraining can help, but requires retaining historical data. ACIL addresses this tension through an analytic learning approach inspired by linear problems.

The paper gives “absolute memorization” a precise meaning: an ACIL update using current data produces the same result as its corresponding joint-learning procedure using both current and historical samples. The authors prove this equality theoretically. The guarantee concerns equivalence to that joint-learning counterpart, so it provides a concrete reference for what preserving past knowledge means.

The privacy claim is specifically tied to avoiding storage and reuse of historical examples. Experiments report competitive accuracy and nearly identical results across incremental settings ranging from 5 to 50 phases. ACIL also outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods in the reported 25- and 50-phase scenarios. These findings suggest particular value when learning is divided into many successive updates.
neurips-2022-acil-analytic-class-increme.tldr: ACIL preserves equivalence to its joint-learning counterpart while learning new classes without retaining historical examples.

paragraphs: Fairness research often examines average predictions, but averages alone do not describe how predictions behave across a distribution. This paper focuses on quantiles, which describe different positions within that distribution. It learns real-valued quantile functions subject to demographic parity with respect to sensitive attributes, such as race or gender, and uses them to construct prediction intervals.

The approach combines optimal transport and functional synchronization to coordinate the fairness adjustment. The authors establish theoretical guarantees of distribution-free coverage and exact fairness for the resulting intervals. Coverage concerns whether an interval contains the outcome being predicted; fairness here refers specifically to the demographic-parity requirement used in the framework.

The paper also provides a practical pipeline that pairs flexible quantile regression methods with an efficient post-processing adjustment. This makes the fairness mechanism usable alongside different quantile predictors. Benchmark experiments report superior empirical performance, and the authors use the results to investigate the relationship between fairness and accuracy. The contribution therefore connects fairness across predicted distributions with uncertainty expressed through intervals.
neurips-2022-conformalized-fairness-via-.tldr: The paper constructs prediction intervals from fair quantiles, with theoretical guarantees of coverage and demographic parity.

paragraphs: This paper develops a general-purpose Bayesian inference algorithm for situations where likelihood evaluations are expensive. Its starting point is Langevin sampling, which includes a stochastic term in its update equation. The proposed method replaces that term with a deterministic term based on a density gradient, changing how the collection of sampling particles moves.

To obtain that gradient, the method estimates the particle density from the particles’ current positions using a normalizing flow. The flow supplies a differentiable density model, allowing density information to guide the updates. The authors emphasize the model’s generalization properties in high dimensions, where representing the evolving particle distribution is an important part of the approach.

The normalizing flow serves additional roles through preconditioning and flow-based Metropolis–Hastings updates, which the authors use to accelerate convergence. Across several examples, the complete method is competitive with state-of-the-art sampling methods. The stated result supports combining learned density information with sampling updates for expensive inference problems; it is an empirical competitiveness claim across those examples.
neurips-2022-deterministic-langevin-mont.tldr: A normalizing flow supplies density gradients and sampling updates for a Bayesian inference method competitive on several examples.

paragraphs: Online learning becomes harder when conditions change during the learning process. Dynamic regret and adaptive regret are two ways to evaluate performance in these non-stationary settings. Existing methods commonly maintain several base learners and use a second algorithm to track which learner is performing best as new observations arrive.

That ensemble structure creates a computational cost in online convex optimization. With a logarithmic number of active learners, a method may need several projections onto the feasible domain each round. Projection enforces the constraints on a decision, and it can become the main computational bottleneck when those constraints define a complicated domain.

The paper develops methods for dynamic and adaptive regret that require just one projection per round, together with one gradient query and one function evaluation. Its approach adapts a reduction mechanism from parameter-free online learning to the changing-environment setting. Empirical studies support the theoretical findings. The contribution makes adaptation less expensive in terms of repeated constraint-enforcement operations, while retaining a regret-based treatment of performance.
neurips-2022-efficient-methods-for-non-s.tldr: The proposed online learning methods handle changing environments with only one projection, gradient query, and function evaluation per round.

paragraphs: Decision-focused learning trains predictions with the eventual optimization decision in mind. This is useful when an optimization problem depends on unknown quantities that a model must estimate. Existing approaches often require convex problems, or problems that can be conveniently relaxed into convex form, and repeatedly solving and differentiating through optimization can make training expensive.

SO-EBM represents the original optimization problem through a differentiable layer based on energy functions. This replaces the use of optimality conditions to define an implicit optimization layer. Its coupled training objective has two roles: a maximum-likelihood loss captures where the optimum lies, while a distribution-based regularizer captures the broader shape of the optimization landscape.

For efficient training, the authors introduce a self-normalized importance sampler with a Gaussian mixture proposal. They evaluate the method on power scheduling, COVID-19 resource allocation, and a nonconvex adversarial security game, reporting effectiveness and efficiency. Together, these components address both how to represent a decision problem during learning and how to train that representation without relying on the usual implicit-layer construction.
neurips-2022-end-to-end-stochastic-optim.tldr: SO-EBM uses energy functions and sampling to make decision-focused learning applicable and efficient across several stochastic optimization applications.

paragraphs: A deployed model may encounter data unlike its training data, making its original performance estimates unreliable. Assessing the change is especially difficult when the new data has no labels. This paper addresses that monitoring problem by considering shifts in labels and input features together, instead of treating either source of change in isolation.

The proposed Sparse Joint Shift model allows the labels and a small number of features to shift jointly. It unifies and extends existing models of label shift and sparse covariate shift. The authors give mathematical conditions under which this shift is identifiable, meaning the available information can determine the shift within the proposed model.

The SEES framework uses this formulation to characterize the distribution change and estimate predictive performance without labels from the new data. Experiments span several real-world datasets, machine learning models, and shifts. Reported improvements in shift estimation error reach an order of magnitude over existing approaches. That result concerns estimation of the shift; the framework’s broader purpose is to make unlabeled deployment monitoring more informative.
neurips-2022-estimating-and-explaining-m.tldr: SEES estimates distribution shifts and model performance without new labels under a model where labels and a few features shift jointly.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel offers a way to study neural network behavior. In the infinite-width limit, it stays fixed, along with its underlying feature map. Finite-width networks can instead learn features early in training before entering a phase where the kernel changes little. This paper examines how adversarial training affects that evolution.

The authors empirically compare kernels during standard and adversarial training. They find that adversarial training rapidly produces a different kernel and feature map. In their experiments, this learned kernel provides adversarial robustness even when the training subsequently performed on top of it is non-robust. This connects robustness to the representation developed during training.

They also investigate adversarial training with a fixed kernel, reporting 76.1% robust accuracy on CIFAR-10 against PGD attacks with a perturbation level of 4/255. The result is specific to that evaluation setting. Together, the findings distinguish the role of learning a kernel from the role of training a classifier using one, helping clarify how both stages can contribute to observed adversarial robustness.
neurips-2022-evolution-of-neural-tangent.tldr: An empirical study finds that adversarial training rapidly learns a distinct neural tangent kernel that can itself support robustness.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decisions when losses change adversarially and the learner observes losses only for state-action pairs it visits. This limited information is called bandit feedback. The objective is low regret: avoiding excessive accumulated loss relative to the comparison policy used in the analysis, despite the changing losses.

The authors investigate Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader, a method whose implementation requires solving an offline planning problem. They overcome difficulties in its analysis and establish near-optimal regret in the episodic, finite-horizon setting. They also extend the analysis to delayed bandit feedback, obtaining order-optimal regret when observations arrive after the corresponding decisions.

A further result addresses communicating adversarial Markov decision processes with stochastic transitions over an infinite horizon. The authors provide the first no-regret algorithm for that setting with bandit feedback. Its computational efficiency assumes access to an offline planning oracle. The contribution therefore combines regret guarantees with a planning-based implementation route, and shows that this approach extends to delayed feedback and continuing interactions.
neurips-2022-follow-the-perturbed-leader.tldr: Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader achieves strong regret guarantees for adversarial decision processes, including delayed feedback and a continuing-interaction setting.

paragraphs: Gaussian differential privacy describes privacy guarantees using a single parameter and offers useful bounds when multiple private computations are combined. Some familiar mechanisms already satisfy this privacy notion, even though their guarantees were originally expressed in another framework. The paper develops tools to recognize and measure those existing Gaussian privacy properties.

The authors study the asymptotic behavior of privacy profiles and derive a criterion for identifying algorithms with Gaussian differential privacy. For qualifying algorithms, they provide an efficient way to narrow down the optimal privacy parameter, μ, with an arbitrarily small, quantifiable error margin. They also give a post-processing procedure that strengthens the guarantees of nonqualifying algorithms until they meet the Gaussian condition.

As an application, the paper proves that every ε-differentially private algorithm also has Gaussian differential privacy. It then combines its measurement procedure with the Gaussian composition theorem to handle repeated private computations. This connects previously established privacy guarantees to a framework that the authors show can make composition analysis more convenient and powerful than traditional standard and advanced composition theorems.
neurips-2022-identification-amplificatio.tldr: The paper provides methods to identify, measure, and obtain Gaussian differential privacy, enabling its use for existing private algorithms.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning lets related tasks share knowledge, but sharing can sometimes harm generalization. This paper investigates spurious correlations as one possible cause. A feature that genuinely helps determine one task’s label may be merely correlated with another task’s label, so sharing it can create an unreliable shortcut for the second task.

The authors also examine confounders linking task labels. Given such confounders, they show theoretically and empirically that multi-task models are prone to using noncausal knowledge from other tasks. Their proposed MT-CRL framework separates knowledge into neural modules and applies an invariance-based regularizer designed for multi-task learning to learn which modules are causally related to each task.

Experiments across Multi-MNIST, MovieLens, Taskonomy, CityScape, and NYUv2 report an average performance improvement of 5.5%, along with evidence that MT-CRL alleviates spurious correlations. The findings support more selective sharing: the framework aims to retain the benefits of shared knowledge while distinguishing which pieces are appropriate for each task. Its causal interpretation is tied to the problem structure studied in the paper.
neurips-2022-improving-multi-task-genera.tldr: MT-CRL separates shared knowledge into modules and regularizes their use to reduce harmful spurious correlations across tasks.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good settings of a black-box function when each evaluation is expensive. Extending it to many input dimensions is difficult: the paper reports that leading high-dimensional approaches can lose performance as dimensionality grows. Some also risk failure when assumptions that cannot be verified do not hold.

BAxUS addresses this problem by adapting the space in which it searches. It uses a family of nested random subspaces, allowing the scope of optimization to change as learning proceeds. Nesting connects these search spaces rather than treating each as an unrelated choice. The central design decision is therefore to make the search space adjustable to the problem.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees addressing the risk of failure described for earlier approaches. A comprehensive evaluation also finds better results than state-of-the-art methods across a broad set of applications. These findings support adaptive subspaces as a way to improve high-dimensional Bayesian optimization. The paper’s practical relevance is to expensive searches where deciding how much of the input space to explore is itself consequential.
neurips-2022-increasing-the-scope-as-you.tldr: BAxUS adapts Bayesian optimization through nested random subspaces, with theoretical guarantees and improved results across evaluated applications.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses evaluations carefully when a black-box function is costly to evaluate. Information-theoretic methods guide that choice by asking what an evaluation could reveal about the optimum. Earlier approaches examine uncertainty either about the input where the optimum occurs or about the optimal output value.

Joint Entropy Search considers those two quantities together. Its acquisition function measures information about the joint distribution of the optimal input and output. To incorporate that information, it conditions on imagined optimal input-output pairs and considers the resulting reduction in entropy. This treats uncertainty about location and value as a connected decision-making target.

The implementation primarily uses standard Gaussian process machinery, avoiding complex approximations commonly associated with information-theoretic approaches. The authors report minimal computational overhead, improved decision-making, and state-of-the-art performance among information-theoretic methods across a broad collection of tasks. The contribution is a practical way to use a richer description of the unknown optimum when deciding where the next expensive evaluation should take place.
neurips-2022-joint-entropy-search-for-ma.tldr: Joint Entropy Search selects evaluations using uncertainty about both the optimal input and its value.

paragraphs: Crop management involves decisions whose consequences unfold over time and depend on environmental conditions. Reinforcement learning can learn such decision policies, but it needs many training examples. Prior work has used crop growth simulators, often restricting learning to one crop, one year, and one management practice.

CyclesGym expands that setting through an environment built on the Cycles crop growth model. It supports multiple crops and years, enabling policies to consider longer-term agricultural consequences. Modular tools define the information available to the learner and the rewards used to assess decisions. Weather generators and support for complex actions allow a wider range of management scenarios.

The paper presents multi-year case studies involving nitrogen fertilization and crop planning to demonstrate reinforcement learning’s potential as an agricultural optimization tool. For researchers, the environment provides a benchmark grounded in agricultural decision problems. Its main contribution is the ability to investigate coordinated, long-term management in simulation, extending beyond the narrow planning scope of the earlier environments described in the abstract.
neurips-2022-learning-long-term-crop-man.tldr: CyclesGym supports reinforcement learning for multi-year, multi-crop management, demonstrated through fertilization and crop-planning case studies.

paragraphs: Sensory studies often begin with features selected by researchers, although the relevant features of complex natural scenes may be unknown. This paper instead uses retinal responses to natural movies to investigate represented information. Time within a movie acts as a proxy for the many scene features changing together, avoiding a full parameterization of the movie.

An encoder-decoder learns from the activity of a large population of salamander retinal ganglion cells. The encoder compresses that activity into a low-dimensional latent representation, and the decoder uses the representation to generate the corresponding movie frame. This task-agnostic architecture lets the researchers examine how information about a natural scene is organized in the compressed space.

Comparing responses to three movies, the authors find that a temporal representation learned from one can represent time in another, with resolution reaching 17 milliseconds. They also find that static textures and velocity features work synergistically in this encoding. The findings support a transferable, low-dimensional representation combining appearance and motion; the proposed behavioral relevance of the represented features remains presumptive.
neurips-2022-learning-low-dimensional-ge.tldr: An encoder-decoder reveals transferable, low-dimensional temporal representations in salamander retinal responses to natural movies.

paragraphs: Machine learning force fields aim to describe atomic interactions accurately while remaining fast enough for computational chemistry and materials science. Equivariant message-passing networks have achieved strong accuracy, but their computational cost and scalability remain challenges. Many pass only two-body messages, tying the richness of their features closely to the number of message-passing layers.

MACE introduces higher-order messages into an equivariant network. These messages represent interactions involving more atoms within a single exchange of information. The authors demonstrate an improved learning law and show that using four-body messages reduces the required message-passing iterations to one. This changes how the network obtains expressive features without requiring repeated rounds of message passing.

The resulting model is described as fast and highly parallelizable. On the rMD17 and 3BPA benchmarks, it reaches or exceeds state-of-the-art accuracy. Those results connect the architectural choice to both predictive quality and computational practicality. The central contribution is to enrich the content of individual messages so that accurate interatomic modeling can be achieved with fewer sequential exchanges.
neurips-2022-mace-higher-order-equivaria.tldr: MACE uses higher-order atomic messages to achieve strong force-field accuracy with a single message-passing iteration.

paragraphs: A learned environment model can help reinforcement learning agents reason about future outcomes before gathering more real experience. Extending this idea to cooperating agents is difficult because multi-agent environments are complex. Errors in a learned model can accumulate across imagined steps and interfere with learning, making straightforward model-based approaches challenging.

The paper proposes an implicit model-based method built around multi-agent value decomposition. Agents interact with a learned virtual environment and imagine future states in a latent representation. They then use those imagined states to evaluate the current state. This gives future-oriented information a direct role in assessing what the agents should do now.

The authors state that the approach can be applied to any multi-agent value-decomposition method. Experiments in different partially observable decision-process domains show improved sample efficiency, meaning learning makes better use of collected experience. The stated evidence supports latent imagination as a useful addition to cooperative learning in those settings, while the motivation emphasizes the difficulty of learning reliable environment models when several agents interact.
neurips-2022-mingling-foresight-with-ima.tldr: The method adds latent-space imagination to multi-agent value decomposition and improves sample efficiency in tested partially observable domains.

paragraphs: Detecting objects in outdoor LiDAR point clouds requires both broad spatial context and fine detail. Objects vary substantially in size, so a detector needs information at different ranges. Window-based transformers can capture distant relationships, but the paper identifies a tendency to blur the detailed information needed for accurate detection.

MsSVT addresses this by dividing attention heads into groups, with each group attending over a particular range. Their outputs are merged into features that combine multiple scales. This division assigns different spatial responsibilities within the transformer, allowing local detail and longer-range information to contribute to the same final representation.

The authors also introduce chessboard sampling to reduce computation in three-dimensional voxel windows and use hash maps for sparse voxel sampling and gathering. These efficiency measures accompany the mixed-scale attention design. A single-stage detector built with MsSVT outperforms state-of-the-art two-stage detectors on Waymo in the reported evaluation. The result supports the value of combining spatial scales while making the underlying sparse processing efficient.
neurips-2022-mssvt-mixed-scale-sparse-vo.tldr: MsSVT combines attention at multiple spatial ranges with efficient sparse processing to improve LiDAR-based 3D detection.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a pattern observed in trained classifiers: features from the same class concentrate around a class mean, and different class means form a structured arrangement aligned with the final classifier. This paper asks why that pattern appears when the final features are normalized, a common practice in representation learning.

The analysis uses an unconstrained feature model and places both features and classifiers on spheres. This turns the classification loss into a nonconvex optimization problem over a product of spheres. Within that model, the authors prove that the only global minimizers are neural-collapse solutions. Every other critical point is a strict saddle with a direction of negative curvature.

This establishes a favorable optimization landscape for the stated mathematical formulation: nonoptimal critical points have directions along which the objective can decrease. Experiments with practical deep networks corroborate the theory and show that feature normalization can produce better representations faster. The theoretical conclusion is specifically about the simplified feature model, while the experiments connect its geometric predictions to observed network behavior.
neurips-2022-neural-collapse-with-normal.tldr: Under a spherical feature model, neural-collapse solutions are the only global optima, and all other critical points are strict saddles.

paragraphs: Sharing a learned representation across reinforcement learning tasks can improve sample efficiency, but explaining that benefit mathematically is difficult. Earlier analyses often assumed that the representation was already known or came from a linear function class. Those restrictions leave a gap between the theory and common practice with nonlinear models such as neural networks.

The paper introduces Generalized Functional Upper Confidence Bound, or GFUCB. An agent handles multiple contextual bandits or Markov decision processes concurrently and learns a shared representation from a specified function class. The analysis addresses challenges including generalization and the construction of confidence bounds in an abstract function space.

The authors theoretically establish benefits of multi-task representation learning with general function classes for bandits and for linear Markov decision processes. Generality of the representation class therefore coexists with a linear-MDP setting for that part of the theory. Experiments using neural-network representations demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The contribution broadens the theoretical treatment of learned representations while retaining an explicit account of the decision-process setting.
neurips-2022-provable-general-function-c.tldr: GFUCB provides theoretical support for shared representations from general function classes in multi-task bandits and linear MDPs.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains from previously collected experience without interacting with the physical environment. That restriction makes it difficult to learn about situations outside the recorded data. State-based approaches can use a learned dynamics model to predict additional transitions, but image-based agents need corresponding visual observations to benefit from that expansion.

S2P, or State2Pixel, supplies this connection through a generative model that synthesizes agent images from states. A dynamics model can predict transitions in state space, and S2P can turn those predicted states into pixels. This allows image-based learning to use virtual experience generated through the more compact state representation.

The authors report that S2P-based image synthesis improves image-based offline reinforcement learning and generalizes strongly to unseen tasks in their experiments. The contribution is a bridge between two forms of experience: states used for predicting transitions and images used by the learner. It gives model-based data augmentation a route into visual offline learning while preserving the setting’s reliance on logged experience during training.
neurips-2022-s2p-state-conditioned-image.tldr: S2P converts predicted states into images so visual offline reinforcement learning can benefit from model-generated experience.

paragraphs: Concentration inequalities bound how far random observations can depart from their expected behavior. Different bounds exploit different properties of the observations. The paper highlights a trade-off: the kl inequality is tighter for Bernoulli variables, while Empirical Bernstein can be tighter for low-variance variables taking values inside a bounded interval.

The proposed split-kl inequality applies to sums of independent bounded random variables. It combines the combinatorial strength of the kl approach with sensitivity to low variance, aiming to retain the advantages of both. The authors also discuss using the inequality to bound excess losses, which measure the additional loss associated with a learning choice relative to a reference.

A further contribution is a PAC-Bayes version of split-kl, extending the idea to a framework for learning guarantees. The paper compares it with several existing PAC-Bayes inequalities using a synthetic example and multiple UCI datasets. These comparisons examine how the new bound behaves alongside alternatives. The central contribution is the construction of a bound that can exploit distributional structure and low variance together.
neurips-2022-split-kl-and-pac-bayes-spli.tldr: Split-kl combines strengths of kl and variance-sensitive concentration bounds, with a PAC-Bayes extension for learning guarantees.

paragraphs: Recommendation benchmarks can be limited by small datasets or narrow records of user behavior. Tenrec addresses both concerns with a publicly available collection covering four recommendation scenarios. It contains approximately five million users and 140 million interactions, providing a setting for evaluating recommendation methods at a substantial scale.

The collection includes positive feedback such as clicks, likes, shares, and follows, together with true negative feedback. It also provides features beyond user and item identifiers. Users and items overlap across the four scenarios, making the relationships between scenarios part of the data. These properties support a wider range of questions than a dataset recording only one kind of positive interaction.

The authors evaluate Tenrec on ten recommendation tasks, running several classical baseline models for each. This demonstrates its use across multiple tasks rather than establishing a single recommendation method as the contribution. The paper presents Tenrec as a potentially useful benchmark for many popular recommendation problems, with its breadth coming from the combination of scale, varied feedback, and overlapping scenarios.
neurips-2022-tenrec-a-large-scale-multip.tldr: Tenrec provides large-scale, varied recommendation feedback across four overlapping scenarios and is evaluated on ten tasks.

paragraphs: Ordinary K-means can be expressed using distances to cluster centers or using distances among observations, with equivalent formulations in Euclidean space. This paper studies what changes when each observation is itself a probability distribution. It uses Wasserstein distance, an optimal-transport metric, to compare these distribution-valued observations.

The geometry of Wasserstein space creates difficulties for barycenters, the counterparts of cluster centers. Their regularity and robustness issues can make them poor representatives of the distributions assigned to a cluster. The authors investigate a direct distance-based K-means formulation and its semidefinite programming relaxation as alternatives that can recover the underlying cluster labels.

For Gaussian distributions, the paper proves exact recovery by the relaxed method when clusters are sufficiently separated under the 2-Wasserstein metric. This is a conditional recovery guarantee, with separation playing a central role. Simulations and real-data examples also show that distance-based clustering can outperform centroid-based K-means for distributions and images. The findings demonstrate why an equivalence familiar from ordinary geometry should not be assumed for distribution-valued data.
neurips-2022-wasserstein-k-means-for-clu.tldr: Distance-based Wasserstein K-means avoids problematic distributional centers and has exact-recovery guarantees for sufficiently separated Gaussian clusters.

paragraphs: Online distillation trains several peer models together so that each can learn from the others. This combines collaboration and training in one stage, but maintaining multiple models consumes memory. Their diversity also matters: the framework must provide useful differences among peers for knowledge exchange to be effective.

Weighted Mutual Learning addresses these concerns through a hierarchy in which models share different network parts. Structured pruning creates varied peer models while reducing memory requirements. The method also estimates the relative importance of peers through a bi-level formulation with a closed-form result, allowing knowledge exchange to weight peers instead of simply averaging them.

Experiments across different deep neural networks show that the framework outperforms existing online distillation methods in the reported comparisons. A single training run also produces pruned models at several sizes, with competitive results against existing channel-pruning methods. The approach therefore links collaborative learning with model compression: pruning shapes the group of learners, and weighted collaboration supports the quality of the resulting models.
neurips-2022-weighted-mutual-learning-wi.tldr: Weighted Mutual Learning combines diverse pruned peers and learned peer weights to improve online distillation while reducing memory needs.

paragraphs: Zero-sum stochastic games describe opposing decision-makers whose interactions evolve across states. Much work focuses on Nash equilibria, but the paper notes that their existence is not guaranteed when state-level payoffs lack convex-concave structure. It instead studies Stackelberg equilibria, using a leader-follower formulation for which existence is guaranteed in the setting considered.

The authors go beyond existing non-stationary equilibrium results by proving the existence of recursive, or Markov-perfect, Stackelberg equilibria. They provide necessary and sufficient conditions for a policy profile to have this property. They also show that value iteration can compute such equilibria in weakly polynomial time, connecting the existence result to an explicit computational method.

The paper then applies the framework to pricing and allocating goods over time. It constructs a game whose recursive Stackelberg equilibria correspond to recursive competitive equilibria in a large class of stochastic Fisher markets. Experiments illustrate how the method solves consumption-savings problems in those markets. This application gives the game-theoretic results an economic interpretation involving repeated allocation decisions under uncertainty.
neurips-2022-zero-sum-stochastic-stackel.tldr: The paper proves and computes recursive Stackelberg equilibria, then connects them to dynamic allocation in stochastic Fisher markets.
